questions.stem: ‘When it is raining, peacocks dance.’ Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?
options: Peacocks dance only when it is raining.
When peacocks dance, it is raining.
When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.

steps.title: What a conditional sentence promises
steps.body: A sentence of the form "when $P$, then $Q$" is a conditional statement. $P$ is the condition (the antecedent) and $Q$ is the result (the consequent). It makes exactly one promise: every time $P$ happens, $Q$ happens. It says nothing about what happens when $P$ does not happen, and nothing about where $Q$ can come from otherwise. The one rule: a conditional $P \to Q$ is equivalent to its contrapositive $\neg Q \to \neg P$ and to nothing else among the four rearrangements.

steps.title: Name the two parts here
steps.body: Let $R$ = "it is raining" and $D$ = "peacocks dance". The sentence is $R \to D$. Raining is the condition, dancing is the result.

steps.title: Write each option in symbols
steps.body:
A: "dance only when raining" means $D 	o R$ (the converse). B: "when they dance, it is raining" is also $D 	o R$. C: "not dancing implies not raining" is $
eg D 	o 
eg R$ (the contrapositive). D: "not raining implies not dancing" is $
eg R 	o 
eg D$ (the inverse).

steps.title: Test each against the one promise
steps.body: Take a day when it is not raining but the peacocks dance anyway (for example, they dance at a mating season). The original sentence is still true, because it only speaks about rainy days. On that day $D \to R$ is false, and $\neg R \to \neg D$ is false. So A, B and D can fail while the sentence holds. In every world where the sentence holds, a non-dancing peacock means the rain condition cannot have occurred, since rain would have forced dancing. So C always holds. The answer is option C.

shortcut.body: Flip and negate both parts: "if P then Q" becomes "if not Q then not P". Only that rearrangement is guaranteed. Under 30 seconds: spot the option that starts with "not dancing" and ends with "not raining". Safe whenever the sentence is a plain if-then.

traps.text: The word "only when" reverses the direction: "$D$ only when $R$" means $D \to R$, which is the converse. Peacocks may dance on dry days too.
This is the same converse in plain words. Seeing dancing does not prove rain, just as a wet road does not prove a downpour.
The inverse negates both parts but keeps the direction. It claims rain is the only cause of dancing, which the sentence never says.

recognize.clues: The sentence "When it is raining, peacocks dance" has the form when P then Q, and the question asks what is necessarily true based only on it, so the task is to pick the valid rearrangement.
recognize.contrast: A statement with "only when" reverses the arrow. "Dance only when raining" says dancing leads to rain, which is the converse of the given sentence, so check which part follows "when".

check.body: Test by building worlds. A dry day with dancing peacocks keeps the original sentence true, and on that day options A, B and D are all false. For option C, a world with rain and a peacock that is not dancing would break the original sentence, so no allowed world defeats C.

If the alarm does not ring, the guard does not wake up.

questions.stem: Water : P :: Food : Q. Choose the P and Q combination from the options below to form a meaningful analogy.

steps.title: What an analogy asks
steps.body: An analogy "$A : B :: C : D$" says the relation between $A$ and $B$ is the same as the relation between $C$ and $D$. To solve it, state the relation in one short sentence using the first pair, then apply that same sentence to the second pair. The pair must also match in kind: a thing, a need, a state.

steps.title: Find the relation from the given words
steps.body: Water and thirst: water is the thing that removes the need called thirst. Food and hunger: food removes the need called hunger. So the relation is "the thing that satisfies the need".

steps.title: Apply it to the options
steps.body: Option A gives Water : Thirst and Food : Hunger, the same relation twice, and thirst and hunger are both needs. Option B puts "Drink" (an action or another name for the liquid) beside "Hunger", so the two pairs differ in kind. Option C pairs Thirst with Satiated, a feeling after eating, so the second pair does not match the first. Option D (Wet, Critic) has no relation. The answer is option A.

shortcut.body: Say the relation aloud: "water cures thirst, food cures hunger". Both blanks must be needs, and only option A has two needs. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Hunger is right for Q, but "Drink" is a verb or a synonym of water, not the need water satisfies. A mixed pair breaks the matching relation.
Thirst is right for P, but "Satiated" names the state after eating, whereas the first pair names the need before drinking. Both blanks have to follow the same relation.
Wet is a property water has and Critic is unrelated to food; the pairs share no relation. A word that merely sounds loosely associated is not an analogy.

recognize.clues: The format "Water : P :: Food : Q" gives one known word on each side and two blanks, so one relation has to serve both pairs and the options supply a word for each blank.
recognize.contrast: A word that is merely associated with the first word, such as Wet for water, is not the same as a word linked by the relation. Say the relation aloud and check that both blanks obey it.

check.body: Run the relation backwards. Thirst is removed by water, and hunger is removed by food, so "thirst : water :: hunger : food" should read in exactly the same way. Mixed options such as Drink with Hunger fail this reverse reading because the two blanks are different kinds of word.

questions.stem: Two tiles are missing in Panel I. Which one of the options in Panel II is the appropriate choice for the missing tiles?
questions.figure: Panel I is a 3 by 3 arrangement of tiles, and each tile is a 3 by 3 block of dots, open (o) or filled (#), written row by row. Row 1 of tiles: [o## / ### / ###], [ooo / ooo / oo#], [o## / o## / o##]. Row 2: [oo# / oo# / oo#], [oo# / o## / o##], then one missing tile. Row 3: [oo# / oo# / o##], [### / ### / ###], then one missing tile. The two missing tiles are the right column, rows 2 and 3, drawn as one dashed tall box. Panel II shows four tall boxes, each with an upper tile for row 2 and a lower tile for row 3: (i) upper [o## / o## / ###], lower [ooo / oo# / oo#]; (ii) upper [o## / o## / o##], lower [ooo / oo# / oo#]; (iii) upper [o## / o## / ###], lower [oo# / oo# / oo#]; (iv) upper [o## / o## / o##], lower [oo# / oo# / o##].

diagram.alt: The 3 by 3 arrangement of dot tiles with the third column of rows 2 and 3 missing, and the four candidate pairs (i) to (iv).

solutionDiagram.alt: The same tiles replaced by their filled-dot counts, forming the magic square 8 1 6 / 3 5 7 / 4 9 2 with every line summing to 15, and the chosen pair (7 and 2 filled dots).

steps.title: Turn pictures into numbers
steps.body: A matrix puzzle hides a rule that every row and column obeys. When the cells are dot patterns, first count what can be counted: here, the number of filled (black) dots in each tile, a number from 0 to 9. The single rule to find is how those nine counts relate across rows and columns.

steps.title: Count the filled dots in the visible tiles
steps.body: Row 1: 8, 1, 6. Row 2: 3, 5, and a missing tile. Row 3: 4, 9, and a missing tile. For example, the middle tile of row 2 is oo# / o## / o## which has $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$ filled dots.

steps.title: Spot the rule: a magic square
steps.body: The first row sums to $8 + 1 + 6 = 15$ and the numbers 1 to 9 appear once each. That is the 3 by 3 magic square, where every row, column and diagonal sums to 15. The first column is $8 + 3 + 4 = 15$ and the middle row is $3 + 5 + ?$, so the missing count in row 2 is $15 - (3 + 5) = 15 - 8 = 7$. In row 3: $4 + 9 + ? = 15$ gives 2.

steps.title: Check the column and diagonals, then pick the option
steps.body: Third column: $6 + 7 + 2 = 15$. Diagonals: $8 + 5 + 2 = 15$ and $6 + 5 + 4 = 15$. We need an upper tile with 7 filled dots and a lower tile with 2. Counts of the options are (i) 7 and 2, (ii) 6 and 2, (iii) 7 and 3, (iv) 6 and 4. Only (i) fits, which is option A.

shortcut.body: Count only the first row (8, 1, 6 = 15), see the magic square 8 1 6 / 3 5 7 / 4 9 2, and read the two missing numbers as 7 and 2. Then count dots in the options; the pair (7, 2) is option A. Roughly 2 minutes. The rule is a guess from three sums, so confirm it with one column before trusting it.

traps.text: Upper tile has 6 dots instead of 7: it reuses the row-1 tile of the same column (o## in every row), directly above the gap, rather than counting. The column sum becomes $6 + 6 + 2 = 14$.

The upper tile (7 dots) is right but the lower tile has 3 dots. It reuses the row-2 first tile oo# / oo# / oo#, which looks natural in a column but has 3 filled dots. The third row then sums to $4 + 9 + 3 = 16$, not 15.
Both tiles are wrong (6 and 4). It looks natural because the lower tile resembles the row-3 first tile, but the row sums are 14 and 17.

recognize.clues: A 3 by 3 panel of dot tiles has the last column of two rows missing, and four candidate pairs fill the gap. Counting the filled dots on each tile turns the picture into numbers with one rule.
recognize.contrast: A matrix of shapes usually repeats or rotates one shape along a row. Here the tiles look different from each other, so counting dots rather than tracking a shape is the method.

check.body: Use the grand total. The nine counts must be the digits 1 to 9 once each, which add to 45, and three rows of 15 also give 45. With 7 and 2 in the gaps the counts are 8, 1, 6, 3, 5, 7, 4, 9, 2: all nine digits appear once and they add to 45. Then count the dots on the chosen tiles: the upper tile of option (i) has 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 and its lower tile has 0 + 1 + 1 = 2.

variation.stem: A 3 by 3 puzzle replaces each cell by a tile, and the number of filled dots on each tile is shown. Row 1 is 2, 7, 6. Row 2 is 9, 5 and a missing tile. Row 3 is 4, 3 and a missing tile. The nine counts follow a single rule that applies to every row and column. Which pair of counts (upper tile, lower tile) completes the last column?

questions.stem: The figure in Panel I below is a grid of cells with four rows and four columns. The numbers on the top and on the left represent the number of cells that are to be shaded in that column and row, respectively. Which one of the options shown in Panel II below represents the grid shaded correctly?
questions.figure: Panel I is an empty 4 by 4 grid. Column clues across the top, left to right: 2, 2, 2, 2. Row clues down the left, top to bottom: 3, 1, 2, 2. Panel II shows four shaded grids, written row by row with # shaded and . white: (i) #.## / .#.# / ..#. / ##.. ; (ii) #.## / .#.. / ..## / ##.. ; (iii) #.## / .##. / ..#. / ##.. ; (iv) #.## / .#.. / ..#. / ##.#

diagram.alt: An empty 4 by 4 grid with column clues 2 2 2 2 and row clues 3 1 2 2, beside four shaded candidate grids (i) to (iv).

solutionDiagram.alt: The four candidate grids with their actual row and column counts written beside them; only option (ii) matches the clues.

steps.title: What the clues mean
steps.body: This is a constraint puzzle. A clue at the top of a column is the number of shaded cells that column must contain, and a clue at the left of a row is the number of shaded cells in that row. A grid is correct only if every row count and every column count equals its clue. Nothing else matters.

steps.title: Write the clues
steps.body: Rows must have 3, 1, 2, 2 shaded cells (total 8). Columns must have 2, 2, 2, 2 (total 8). The totals agree, as they must.

steps.title: Check the rows first
steps.body: Row 2 must have exactly 1 shaded cell. Option (i) row 2 is .#.# with 2 shaded, so it fails. Option (iii) row 2 is .##. with 2 shaded, so it fails. Option (iv) row 4 is ##.# with 3 shaded instead of 2, so it fails. Option (ii) rows count 3, 1, 2, 2 as required.

steps.title: Confirm option (ii) on columns
steps.body: Option (ii) is #.## / .#.. / ..## / ##... Column 1 has rows 1 and 4, column 2 has rows 2 and 4, column 3 has rows 1 and 3, column 4 has rows 1 and 3. Each column has 2 shaded cells, matching 2, 2, 2, 2. The answer is option B.

shortcut.body: Scan only the row with the smallest clue (the 1 in row 2): any option with two shaded cells there is out. That removes (i) and (iii) at once. Then count row 4 of the remaining two. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Columns all come out as 2 2 2 2, which looks right at a glance, but row 2 has two shaded cells where the clue says 1. Check rows as well as columns.
Row 2 has two shaded cells, and column 3 has three while column 4 has only one. It fails both clue sets.
Row 2 and the columns are fine, but row 4 has three shaded cells (##.#) where the clue says 2, and row 3 has only one where the clue says 2.

recognize.clues: Numbers printed along the top and the left of an empty 4 by 4 grid give how many cells to shade in each column and row, and four completed grids are offered to be checked against them.
recognize.contrast: A seating puzzle gives clues about relative positions that you combine into one layout. Here the clues are counts per line, so you verify counts in each option instead of deducing positions.

check.body: Take the complement: swap shaded and white in option (ii). A grid with 4 columns must then have row counts $4 - 3, 4 - 1, 4 - 2, 4 - 2 = 1, 3, 2, 2$ and column counts $4 - 2 = 2$ each. Counting the swapped grid directly gives rows 1, 3, 2, 2 and columns 2, 2, 2, 2, so the two descriptions agree.

questions.stem: ‘When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently.’ If the above statement is true, which one of the following statements is not necessarily true?
options: If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.
If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing.

steps.title: Conditional, contrapositive and weakening
steps.body: A statement "when $P$, then $Q$" ($P \to Q$) promises that $Q$ holds every time $P$ holds. Three rearrangements follow from it: the contrapositive $\neg Q \to \neg P$ (always valid), a weaker result (if $Q$ is "silent and standing" then "silent" alone or "standing" alone also follows), and nothing else. The converse $Q \to P$ is not guaranteed. "Not necessarily true" means: some world makes the original statement true and the option false.

steps.title: Name the parts
steps.body: Let $T$ = teacher in the room, $Q$ = "all students stand silently", which means all are standing and all are silent. The given statement is $T \to (\text{standing} \wedge \text{silent})$.

steps.title: Test A, B and D
steps.body: A says "if some student is not standing silently then the teacher is out", which is the contrapositive $\neg Q \to \neg T$: necessarily true. B keeps only "silent" from the result: necessarily true. D keeps only "standing" from the result: necessarily true.

steps.title: Test C
steps.body: C says "if all students are standing, the teacher is in the room", which is $\text{standing} \to T$, a converse. It can be false: the class stands for the anthem while the teacher is absent, and the original statement is still true because it only describes what happens when the teacher is in. So C is not necessarily true, option C.

shortcut.body: Three options only shrink the result or flip-and-negate; one reverses the arrow. Find the option where the teacher appears as the result instead of the condition: option C. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: This looks like a reversal but is the contrapositive: not (standing silently) forces the teacher to be out. It is necessarily true, so it is the wrong pick for a "not necessarily true" question.
Dropping "standing" leaves a weaker claim ("silent"), which still follows. Candidates mistake a missing detail for a different claim.
Dropping "silently" leaves "standing", which still follows from the original result. A weaker consequent is always safe.

recognize.clues: The sentence "When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently" is a when-then statement, and the phrase "not necessarily true" asks for the option that is not a valid rearrangement of it.
recognize.contrast: The contrapositive flips the arrow and negates both parts, which is valid. The converse flips the arrow without negating, which is not. Check whether the "not" has been applied to both ends.

check.body: Build a world to test. Let the teacher be absent while every student stands for the anthem. The original sentence is still true because it says nothing about the teacher being absent, yet in that world option C has a true condition (all students are standing) and a false conclusion (the teacher is in the room). Separately, assume a student is not standing silently while the teacher is in: the original would force that student to stand silently, a contradiction.

If the pump has not failed, the alarm does not sound.

questions.stem: Combinatorics deals with problems involving counting. For example, “How many distinct arrangements of N distinct objects in M spaces on a circle are possible?” is a typical problem in combinatorics. This kind of counting is sometimes used in the modeling of several physical phenomena. Often, in such models, the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values. Assigning probabilities enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities. Consider the following statements: P: Combinatorics is always invoked in the modeling of physical phenomena. Q: Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities in order to compute average values of physical quantities. Based on the passage above, what can be inferred about statements P and Q?
options: P is False and Q is False
P is False and Q is True
P is True and Q is False
P is True and Q is True

steps.title: What "based on the passage" means
steps.body: An inference question asks whether a statement is supported by the text. A statement is true if the passage says it or entails it; false if the passage says the opposite or only supports a weaker claim. Use no outside knowledge. Watch the quantifier words: "always" claims every case, "some" claims at least one, "sometimes" and "often" claim only part of the cases.

steps.title: Judge P
steps.body: P says combinatorics is always invoked. The passage says counting "is sometimes used" in modelling. "Sometimes" supports "in some cases", not "in every case", so P overclaims. P is false.

steps.title: Judge Q
steps.body: The passage says that in "such models" the combinatorial possibilities are assigned probabilities, and that this "enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities". The word "often" and the opening "sometimes" together match Q: some physical phenomena are modelled by assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities to compute averages. Q is true.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: P is false and Q is true, which is option B.

shortcut.body: Circle the quantifiers: "always" in P against "sometimes/often" in the passage kills P; "some" in Q matches the passage. 30 seconds. Unsafe only when a statement hides a quantifier in a plural noun.

traps.text: Rejecting Q too: it sounds technical, so candidates distrust it. But it restates the second half of the passage word for word with the quantifier "some".
Accepts P and rejects Q, the reverse of the truth. P turns the passage’s "sometimes" into "always", and Q is not an overclaim.
Accepts P because combinatorics is the passage’s topic. But a topic mentioned in the passage is not claimed to be universal in the models.

recognize.clues: A short passage is followed by statements P and Q and the phrase "based on the passage". P contains "always" and Q contains "some", so each statement is judged by its quantifier against the text.
recognize.contrast: This differs from a conditional-statements question, where you rearrange an if-then. Here no arrow exists, and the work is to compare how strong each claim is with how strong the passage is.

check.body: Test P by imagining a physical process the passage lets stand, such as a model with no counting step at all. Nothing in the text rules it out, so "always" can fail. For Q, the passage itself describes models in which probabilities are assigned to the counted possibilities to get average values, which is at least one case.

options: P is False and Q is False
P is False and Q is True
P is True and Q is False

questions.stem: In the 2020 summer Olympics’ Javelin throw finals, Neeraj Chopra exhibited a spectacular performance to win the gold medal. The silver medal was won by Jakub Vadlejch and the bronze medal was won by Vitezlav Vesely. There were six rounds of throws with each athlete having one throw per round. The best of all the throws of each athlete is considered for the medal. Following were the observations about the throws: i. The first and second rounds were dominated by Neeraj Chopra with a gold medal performance in his second throw, while the other two athletes did not have any medal winning throws in these rounds. ii. The throws in the last round by both Jakub Vadlejch and Vitezlav Vesely were fouls and were not considered for scoring. iii. After four rounds, Vitezlav Vesely was in the second position and could not improve upon his best throw in the succeeding rounds. iv. In the fourth round, the throw by Jakub Vadlejch was the best in that round. In which round did Vitezlav Vesely have his best throw?

solutionDiagram.alt: Six round boxes for Vesely's best throw: rounds 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 are crossed out with the clue that removes each, and round 3 is left.

steps.title: What is being asked and the rule
steps.body: Each athlete is ranked by the best (longest) single throw over the rounds. We need the round that holds Vesely’s best throw. The method is elimination: list the six rounds as candidates and strike out each one that a clue contradicts.

steps.title: Strike out rounds 1 and 2
steps.body: Clue i: in rounds 1 and 2 the other two athletes had no medal-winning throw. Vesely’s best throw earned the bronze medal, so it cannot be in round 1 or 2.

steps.title: Strike out round 6
steps.body: Clue ii: Vesely’s last-round throw was a foul and did not count, so his best is not in round 6.

steps.title: Strike out round 5
steps.body: Clue iii: after four rounds Vesely was already second and "could not improve upon his best throw" afterwards. So his best throw is within rounds 1 to 4; round 5 is out.

steps.title: Strike out round 4, leaving round 3
steps.body: Clue iv: in round 4, Jakub’s throw was the best of that round, so Vesely’s round-4 throw was shorter than Jakub’s. If Vesely’s best were in round 4, then Jakub’s round-4 throw would be longer than Vesely’s best, putting Jakub ahead of Vesely after four rounds. But Vesely was second after four rounds, so Jakub was behind him, not ahead. Round 4 is out. The remaining round is the third, option A.

shortcut.body: Write 1 to 6, cross out 1, 2 (clue i), 6 (foul), 5 (no improvement after four rounds), and 4 (Jakub beat him there). Round 3 is left. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Round 4 tempts because clue iii says "after four rounds". But clue iv shows Jakub out-threw him in round 4, which would put Jakub ahead of Vesely at that point.
Round 5 ignores the phrase "could not improve upon his best throw in the succeeding rounds", which means no later round improves it.
Round 6 ignores clue ii: the last-round throw was a foul and counts for nothing.

recognize.clues: Four numbered observations about six rounds and three named athletes, and a question asking in which round one athlete had his best throw, so the clues rule rounds out one by one.
recognize.contrast: A seating puzzle fixes people in relative positions and needs a full table. Here the unknown is one position in a sequence, so striking out candidates is faster than building a table.

check.body: Build a made-up schedule that obeys all four clues with the best throw in round 3. Say Chopra throws 87 m in round 2; Vesely throws 85 m in round 3 and less elsewhere; Vadlejch throws 82 m in round 4, the round's longest, then 86 m in round 5, and both fouls come in round 6. After four rounds the order is Chopra, Vesely, Vadlejch, and Vesely cannot improve. The medals then match the passage. The lengths are invented only to show the clues can all hold together.

questions.stem: Bird : Nest :: Bee : _______. Select the correct option to complete the analogy.

steps.title: What an analogy asks
steps.body: In "$A : B :: C : D$", the relation between $A$ and $B$ must equal the relation between $C$ and $D$. First put the known pair into a sentence, then fill the blank so the same sentence holds.

steps.title: State the relation
steps.body: A nest is the home that a bird builds and lives in. So the relation is "animal : the home it makes for itself".

steps.title: Apply to bees and the options
steps.body: The home of a bee colony is a hive, which bees build. A kennel is a home for a dog, built by people. A hammock is a hanging bed. A lair is a wild animal’s den, such as a lion’s. Only hive fits. The answer is option C.

shortcut.body: Say "bird lives in a nest, bee lives in a ___". "Hive" comes instantly. 15 seconds.

traps.text: A kennel is the home of a dog, so it belongs to a different animal. Matching the home to the wrong creature breaks the pair.
A hammock is a bed for a person; it is not an animal’s own home. It shares only the "hanging" image with a nest.
A lair is a den of a wild predator such as a lion or fox. A bee’s home is the hive, so the animal type does not fit.

recognize.clues: The pattern "Bird : Nest :: Bee : blank" pairs an animal with its home, and the four options are different dwellings or shelters, so the animal must match.
recognize.contrast: A hammock is a place to rest, not the home of a particular animal. Tell them apart by asking whether the word names the dwelling of that very animal.

check.body: Look at what each home holds. A nest holds eggs and chicks of a bird, and the matching place for bees holds honey and young bees. Then test the other options on the same question: a kennel holds a dog, a hammock holds a sleeping person and a lair holds a predator, none of which is a bee.

questions.stem: Based only on the conversation below, identify the logically correct inference: “Even if I had known that you were in the hospital, I would not have gone there to see you”, Ramya told Josephine.
options: Ramya knew that Josephine was in the hospital.
Ramya did not know that Josephine was in the hospital.
Ramya and Josephine were once close friends; but now, they are not.
Josephine was in the hospital due to an injury to her leg.

steps.title: Counterfactual sentences
steps.body: A sentence with "had known ... would not have gone" is a past counterfactual: it describes a situation that did not happen in order to make a point. Using "had known" in the past perfect signals that the speaker did not in fact know. "Even if" adds emphasis: even in that imagined case, the result stays the same. An inference must follow from the words alone, with no extra story.

steps.title: Read what the sentence forces
steps.body: Ramya imagines knowing about the hospital stay ("had known"). That imagined state contrasts with reality, so in reality she did not know. This is the only fact the sentence settles.

steps.title: Check the options
steps.body: A says she knew: this reverses the counterfactual. C adds a history of friendship the sentence never mentions. D adds a leg injury; nothing in the sentence names the reason for the hospital stay. Only B is forced. The answer is option B.

shortcut.body: "Had known" in the past perfect means "did not know". Pick the option that says so and discard options that add new facts (friendship, a leg). 30 seconds.

traps.text: Reads "if I had known" as if it said "I knew". The past perfect counterfactual implies the opposite of what it supposes.
Plausible as a story, but the sentence says nothing about earlier friendship. Inference questions allow only what the text forces.
The cause of the hospital visit is not given anywhere; picking it means inventing detail.

recognize.clues: The question says "based only on the conversation" and asks for the logically correct inference. The key words are the past-perfect "had known" and "would not have gone", which carry the information.
recognize.contrast: Conditional statements looks similar because of the if-type wording, but there is no arrow to rearrange here. The tense of the verb, not the logic of P and Q, gives the inference.

check.body: Read the sentence once for each of two options. If the statement that she knew were true, "even if I had known" would be a strange phrase, since nothing is imagined. If the statement that she did not know were true, the phrase reads naturally. Neither the friendship nor the leg injury can be tested at all, because the sentence never mentions them.

questions.stem: If IMAGE and FIELD are coded as FHBNJ and EMFJG respectively then, which one among the given options is the most appropriate code for BEACH?

steps.title: What a letter code is
steps.body: In a letter code, one fixed rule is applied to every word. Possible rules are shifting each letter along the alphabet, reversing the order of the letters, or both. To find the rule, lay one coded word under its original and compare position by position, then confirm it on the second example before using it.

steps.title: Look for the rule on IMAGE
steps.body: IMAGE becomes FHBNJ. Move each letter one step forward in the alphabet: I→J, M→N, A→B, G→H, E→F, giving JNBHF. Now reverse that word: FHBNJ. That matches.

steps.title: Confirm on FIELD
steps.body: FIELD with each letter +1 gives GJFME, and reversing it gives EMFJG, exactly the second code. The rule (shift +1, then reverse) works on both.

steps.title: Apply to BEACH
steps.body: BEACH with +1 gives CFBDI. Reversed, it is IDBFC. That is option B.

shortcut.body: In both examples the first letter of the code is the last letter of the word plus one, and the last letter of the code is the first letter of the word plus one. For BEACH that means the code starts with I (H+1) and ends with C (B+1), which leaves IDBFC and IBCEC. The second letter of the code is the second-last letter of the word plus one, C+1 = D, so IDBFC. About 1 minute.

traps.text: CEADP starts with C (B+1) and so keeps the word in forward order, but the examples reverse the word. It ends in P, which is not B+1.
JGIBC ends with C, which is correct (B+1), but starts with J instead of I (the last letter H plus one). Its middle letters also do not follow the rule.
IBCEC has the right first letter I and the right last letter C, so a two-letter check keeps it. The middle letters should be D, B, F (from C, A, E plus one) and it has B, C, E.

recognize.clues: Two words and their codes are given, and a third word must be coded with the same rule. The codes have the same length as the words, which points to a letter-by-letter rule.
recognize.contrast: Number series also asks for a hidden rule, but works on numbers and gaps. Here the rule acts on letter positions, so look at shifts of position and at the order of the letters.

check.body: Run the rule backwards on the result. Reverse IDBFC to get CFBDI, then move each letter one step back in the alphabet: C to B, F to E, B to A, D to C, I to H. This returns BEACH, so the code is consistent. The competing option IBCEC fails the same test, because undoing it does not return BEACH.

questions.stem: Consider the relationships among P, Q, R, S, and T: P is the brother of Q. S is the daughter of Q. T is the sister of S. R is the mother of Q. The following statements are made based on the relationships given above. (1) R is the grandmother of S. (2) P is the uncle of S and T. (3) R has only one son. (4) Q has only one daughter. Which one of the following options is correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: Family tree: R is the mother of siblings P and Q; Q is the parent of daughters S and T.

steps.title: Blood-relation terms
steps.body: In a family tree an arrow goes from parent to child. Siblings share a parent. A parent’s mother is a grandmother; a parent’s brother is an uncle. A fact like "brother of" gives the gender of the person named first: P is male, T is female (a sister), S is female (a daughter). The gender of Q is not given, and nothing a statement needs may be assumed beyond what is written.

steps.title: Build the tree
steps.body: R is the mother of Q. P is a brother of Q, so P is also a child of R. S is a daughter of Q, and T is a sister of S, so T is a daughter of Q too.

steps.title: Check (1) and (2)
steps.body: (1) R is Q’s mother and Q is S’s parent, so R is S’s grandmother: true. (2) P is the brother of Q, who is the parent of S and T. A parent’s brother is an uncle, so P is the uncle of S and T: true.

steps.title: Check (3) and (4)
steps.body: (3) R has son P. Q could also be a son, because the gender of Q is not given. So "only one son" is not established, and it is not true as a guaranteed statement. (4) Q has two daughters, S and T, so "only one daughter" is false. Only (1) and (2) hold, which is option A.

shortcut.body: Draw R at the top, P and Q as her children, S and T under Q. Read (1) and (2) off the picture; (4) is false because both S and T are Q’s daughters; (3) cannot be confirmed. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Accepts (3) because only P is named as a son. But Q’s gender is not given, so R could have two sons.
Takes (3) as true and misses that (1) and (2) are both forced by the tree. (3) is at best undetermined.
Takes S as the only daughter. T is a sister of S, so T is also a daughter of Q: Q has two daughters.

recognize.clues: Five people are linked by "brother of", "daughter of", "sister of" and "mother of", and four statements about the relationships must be judged. This asks for a family tree.
recognize.contrast: Direction sense also draws a diagram, but the relations here are about generations and gender. Notice that the gender of Q is never given, so some statements cannot be settled.

check.body: Build two concrete families that both fit the facts. In the first, Q is a son: R has two sons, so the claim about only one son fails. In the second, Q is a daughter: R has one son. The claim about the number of sons changes between the families, so it is not forced. The claims about R as grandmother and P as uncle hold in both, and S and T are daughters of Q in both.

questions.stem: According to the map shown in the figure, which one of the following statements is correct? Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.figure: A campus map with north at the top. The vertical 1st Main Road runs through the middle, and the horizontal 5th Cross Road crosses it. North of 5th Cross Road, west of 1st Main Road: Library (upper) and Physics Lab (below it). North of 5th Cross Road, east of 1st Main Road: Canteen (upper) and Hospital (below it). South of 5th Cross Road, west of 1st Main Road: Hostels (upper) and Classrooms (below it). South of 5th Cross Road, east of 1st Main Road: Chemistry Lab. A compass shows N up, S down, W left, E right.

diagram.alt: Campus map with Library and Physics Lab west of 1st Main Road, Canteen and Hospital east of it, all north of 5th Cross Road, and Hostels, Classrooms and Chemistry Lab south of it.

options: The library is located to the northwest of the canteen.
The hospital is located to the east of the chemistry lab.
The chemistry lab is to the southeast of physics lab.
The classrooms and canteen are next to each other.

steps.title: Reading a map
steps.body: On a map with a compass, north is up, south down, east right and west left. To give the direction of $B$ from $A$, ask how far $B$ is to the right or left of $A$ (east or west) and how far above or below it (north or south). If both differ, the direction is a corner such as southeast. If only one differs, it is a pure direction. Buildings in different blocks of a road grid are not "next to" each other.

steps.title: Place the buildings
steps.body: The west column has the Library at top and Physics Lab beneath, then the 5th Cross Road, then Hostels and Classrooms. The east column has Canteen, Hospital, the road, then Chemistry Lab. So Physics Lab is north-west of the junction and Chemistry Lab is south-east of it.

steps.title: Check each statement
steps.body: A: the Library is in the same row as the Canteen but on the west side, so it is west of the canteen, not northwest. B: the Hospital is directly north of the Chemistry Lab (same side of the main road, above the cross road), so not east. C: Chemistry Lab is east of the main road (right) and south of the cross road (below), while Physics Lab is west and north, so the lab is to the southeast of Physics Lab: true. D: Classrooms are far south-west and Canteen is north-east, so they are not adjacent. The answer is option C.

shortcut.body: Locate each building in the quadrant grid (NW, NE, SW, SE of the crossing). Physics Lab is NW, Chemistry Lab is SE, so C. 30 seconds.

traps.text: Library and Canteen sit at the same height, so the direction is due west, not northwest. A corner direction needs a vertical difference too.
The Hospital is straight above the Chemistry Lab, so it is north, not east. Both are on the east side of the road.
Classrooms (south-west) and Canteen (north-east) are on opposite corners across two roads. They are not next to each other.

recognize.clues: A figure with a compass shows buildings on a road grid, and each statement gives a direction between two buildings. That asks for offsets east-west and north-south.
recognize.contrast: Arrangement puzzles also place items by position, but there the positions come from clues in words. Here they are read off the picture, and the only skill is comparing offsets.

check.body: Assign coordinates with the crossing as the origin, east and north positive. Physics Lab is at (-1, +1) and Chemistry Lab at (+1, -1). The difference from Physics Lab to Chemistry Lab is (+2, -2): east and south both. Run the same test on the other statements: Library at (-1, +2) and Canteen at (+1, +2) differ only east-west, so no corner direction is possible there.

questions.stem: In the sequence 6, 9, 14, x, 30, 41, a possible value of $x$ is

steps.title: What a number series is
steps.body: A number series follows one rule that turns each term into the next. The most common test is the difference between neighbours. If the differences are themselves not constant, take the differences of the differences: if those are constant, the series is quadratic in the position. Always check that the guessed rule reproduces every known term, not only the first few.

steps.title: Differences of the known terms
steps.body: From 6 to 9 the step is 3, from 9 to 14 it is 5, and from 30 to 41 it is 11. The steps 3, 5 and 11 are odd numbers, and 3, 5, then 7, 9, 11 form the odd numbers in order.

steps.title: Find x
steps.body: $x = 14 + 7 = 21$. Check the next steps: $21 + 9 = 30$ and $30 + 11 = 41$, both given. The answer is 21, option B.

shortcut.body: Write the gaps: 3, 5, ?, ?, 11. The gaps rise by 2, so the missing gaps are 7 and 9, giving 21. Check by testing the options: only 21 makes the gaps 7 then 9. 30 seconds.

traps.text: With 25 the gaps are 3, 5, 11, 5, 11: the gap falls from 11 to 5, so there is no steady pattern.
With 18 the gaps are 3, 5, 4, 12, 11. A gap of 4 breaks the rising order and 12 then overshoots 11.
With 20 the gaps are 3, 5, 6, 10, 11. Gaps of 6 and 10 are even and skip the odd numbers 7 and 9.

recognize.clues: The series is given with one blank in the middle and the option values test a single rule. The known gaps 3, 5 and 11 are not equal, which points to gaps that grow.
recognize.contrast: Numerical relations also uses numbers, but there the relation is between pairs. Here the relation runs along one list, so test differences before trying products.

check.body: Find a formula for the whole series. The terms 6, 9, 14, 21, 30, 41 are $n^2 + 5$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$, since $1+5, 4+5, 9+5, 16+5, 25+5, 36+5$. That formula gives the fourth term as $16 + 5 = 21$ and reproduces every given term.

questions.stem: In the 4 × 4 array shown below, each cell of the first three rows has either a cross (X) or a number. The number in a cell represents the count of the immediate neighboring cells (left, right, top, bottom, diagonals) NOT having a cross (X). Given that the last row has no crosses (X), the sum of the four numbers to be filled in the last row is
questions.figure: A 4 by 4 array. Row 1: 1, X, 4, 3. Row 2: X, 5, 5, 4. Row 3: 3, X, 6, X. Row 4: four empty cells, all of which hold numbers (no crosses).

diagram.alt: A 4 by 4 array whose first three rows read 1 X 4 3, X 5 5 4 and 3 X 6 X, with the fourth row empty.

solutionDiagram.alt: The completed array with fourth row 2 4 3 2 and the sum 11.

steps.title: The counting rule
steps.body: Every number cell shows how many of its neighbours are not crosses. The neighbours of a cell are the up to eight cells touching it, sideways, up, down and on the diagonals. A cell on an edge or corner has fewer neighbours (5 on an edge, 3 in a corner). To find a number, list the neighbours that exist and count those not marked X.

steps.title: Neighbours of the bottom-left cell (4,1)
steps.body: Its neighbours are (3,1)=3, (3,2)=X, (4,2) in the last row (no cross). Two are not crosses, so the cell is 2.

steps.title: Sum
steps.body: The last row is 2, 4, 3, 2 and the sum is $2 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 11$. The numbers already printed in rows 1 to 3 agree with the rule, which confirms it. The answer is option A.

shortcut.body: Only row 3 touches row 4, so count the crosses in row 3: X at columns 2 and 4. Each bottom cell loses one count per touching cross: starting totals 3, 5, 5, 3 (corner, edge, edge, corner) minus crosses touching gives 2, 4, 3, 2. 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: A total of 10 means exactly one count was lost, for example counting the bottom-edge cell (4,2) as 3 instead of 4 by skipping one of its non-cross neighbours. Treating a printed number such as the 6 at (3,3) as a cross is a worse slip: it lowers the row by 3, to 8. Only cells marked X reduce a count.
A total of 12 comes from missing the diagonal cross (3,4) for the cell (4,3), which leaves that cell at 4 instead of 3. Cross cells touch diagonally too.
A total of 9 loses two counts, for example by treating the printed 3 at (3,1) as a cross: it lowers both (4,1) and (4,2) by one. Count a neighbour as lost only when it is marked X.

recognize.clues: A grid of crosses and counts must be completed by a counting rule that involves all eight neighbouring cells. The last row has no crosses, so only the row above affects it.
recognize.contrast: Arrangement puzzles also fills positions, but through ordering clues. Here the only tool is counting neighbours, so no ordering is needed.

check.body: Verify the printed numbers against the rule. Cell (3,1) shows 3: its neighbours are (2,1)=X, (2,2), (3,2)=X, (4,1), (4,2), five cells with two crosses, giving 3. Cell (3,3) shows 6: eight neighbours with the two crosses at (3,2) and (3,4), giving 6. Both agree only if the last row has no crosses, which supports the numbers filled in.

questions.stem: A survey for a certain year found that 90% of pregnant women received medical care at least once before giving birth. Of these women, 60% received medical care from doctors, while 40% received medical care from other healthcare providers. Given this information, which one of the following statements can be inferred with certainty?

solutionDiagram.alt: One bar of 100 pregnant women split into 54 who saw a doctor, 36 who saw other providers and 10 with no care, with a dashed line at 50 inside the doctor segment.

options: More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor.
Less than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor.
More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at most once from a doctor.
Less than half of the pregnant women received medical care at most once from a doctor.

steps.title: What 'inferred with certainty' asks for
steps.body: A statement can be inferred with certainty only if it is true in every situation the passage allows. If even one allowed situation makes it false, it cannot be inferred. A second rule covers percentages: a percentage always refers to a base group. '90% of pregnant women' has all pregnant women as its base. '60% of these women' has only the 90% who received care as its base. To compare with 'half of the pregnant women', every figure must first be turned into a share of all pregnant women.

steps.title: Put every figure on the same base
steps.body: Take 100 pregnant women. Of them 90 received care at least once. Of those 90, 60% saw a doctor and 40% saw other providers. Since 60% and 40% add to 100%, these two groups cover all 90 women.
steps.tex: 90 \times 0.60 = 54 \text{ women saw a doctor}, \qquad 90 \times 0.40 = 36 \text{ saw other providers}

steps.title: Compare with half
steps.body: Half of 100 is 50, and 54 is more than 50. So more than half of all pregnant women received care from a doctor at least once. This does not depend on how the groups overlap, because the 54 comes straight from the 60% figure. That makes option A certain and option B false.

steps.title: Why C and D cannot be inferred
steps.body: 'At most once from a doctor' counts women whose doctor visits were zero or one. The passage gives who saw a doctor, never how many visits each made. If none of the 54 had a second visit, all 100 women were seen at most once, so C is true and D is false. If all 54 had two or more visits, only 46 were seen at most once, so C is false and D is true. The answer flips with facts the passage does not give, so neither is certain. The answer is option A.

shortcut.body: Multiply the two percentages: 0.9 x 0.6 = 0.54, which is above 0.5, so A. Drop C and D at once, because 'at most once' needs visit counts the passage never gives. About 30 seconds. It is safe whenever the question asks about 'at least once'; it would be unsafe if the doctor share had come out near 50%.

traps.text: Reading '60% of these women' as 60% of the women with the 10% who received no care subtracted again (54 - 10 = 44) double-counts the 10%, because the 10% are already outside the 90% that the 60% is taken from. The correct base gives 54%.

'At most once' and 'at least once' look like a mirror pair, so A's logic seems to carry over. It does not: 'at least once' is settled by who saw a doctor, but 'at most once' needs the count of visits, which the passage never gives.
The same missing visit count rules out D. Its 'less than half' conclusion holds only if most of the 54 women had two or more visits, and the passage is silent on that.

recognize.clues: The question asks which statement can be inferred with certainty from percentages of percentages. The words "at least once" and "at most once" decide which options can be tested.
recognize.contrast: Logical fallacies is close because wrong options look reasonable, but here the check is arithmetic on a common base. The phrase "at most once" needs visit counts that are not given.

check.body: Use a bound instead of rescaling. The 60% is stated, so the doctor group is at least 54 of the 100 women whatever the overlap with other providers. The women outside it number at most 100 - 54 = 46, which is under 50. So the doctor group is more than half in every allowed case.

questions.stem: The country of Zombieland is in distress since more than 75% of its working population is suffering from serious health issues. Studies conducted by competent health experts concluded that a complete lack of physical exercise among its working population was one of the leading causes of their health issues. As one of the measures to address the problem, the Government of Zombieland has decided to provide monetary incentives to those who ride bicycles to work. Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following statements can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: All the working population of Zombieland will henceforth ride bicycles to work.
Riding bicycles will ensure that all of the working population of Zombieland is free of health issues.
The health experts suggested to the Government of Zombieland to declare riding bicycles as mandatory.
The Government of Zombieland believes that riding bicycles is a form of physical exercise.

steps.title: What 'logically inferred with certainty' means here
steps.body: An inference is a statement that the facts of the passage force to be true. 'Based only on the information provided' bans outside knowledge, such as what governments usually do. The test for each option is one question: can the passage be true while this option is false? If yes, the option is an overreach. Words like 'all', 'ensure', 'mandatory' and 'only' are warning signs, because they claim much more than a passage normally supports.

steps.title: List what the passage actually states
steps.body: Fact 1: more than 75% of the working population has serious health issues. Fact 2: experts concluded that a complete lack of physical exercise is one of the leading causes of those issues. Fact 3: as one measure to address the problem, the Government will give money to those who ride bicycles to work. Nothing else is stated.

steps.title: Reject A, B and C
steps.body: A: an incentive rewards people who ride; it forces nobody, so the passage stays true even if few ride. B: lack of exercise is only 'one of the leading causes', and a measure to address a problem is not a guarantee, so nothing ensures that everyone becomes healthy. C: the experts named a cause; the passage never says they advised anything, and the Government chose an incentive, not a compulsion.

steps.title: Why D is forced
steps.body: The cause the experts named is lack of physical exercise, and the Government's measure to address the problem is paying people to cycle. A payment for cycling can address a lack of exercise only if the Government counts cycling as exercise. So the passage cannot be true while the Government fails to hold that belief. The answer is option D.

shortcut.body: Cross out options with strong words: 'all' (A), 'ensure ... all' (B), 'mandatory' (C). The mild option D is the link between the cause and the measure. About 1 minute. The elimination by strong words is a habit, not a law: check that D really connects two facts before trusting it.

traps.text: 'Monetary incentives' read as 'everyone will cycle'. An incentive offers a reward and compels no one, and the passage says nothing about how many will respond.

Hoping the measure cures the problem. The passage says lack of exercise is 'one of the leading causes', so other causes remain, and a measure to 'address' a problem does not promise to remove it for all.
Importing a belief about what experts would recommend. The passage reports the experts' conclusion about a cause only; a recommendation to make cycling mandatory is added by the reader.

recognize.clues: The passage gives a cause and a measure, and the question asks what follows "based only on the information provided" with certainty. Strong words in three of the options are signs of overreach.
recognize.contrast: Logical fallacies names the errors that make options like these tempting. The task here is the reverse: find the one option that the passage supports without any extra assumption.

check.body: Build a world for each of the other three options in which the passage is true and the option is false. A few people take the incentive and the rest do not, which defeats the first. Someone cycles and is still ill from another cause, which defeats the second. The experts only name a cause and the Government has chosen an incentive, which defeats the third. No such world exists for the last option, since the measure only addresses the cause if cycling is counted as exercise.

questions.stem: Given below are four statements. Statement 1: All students are inquisitive. Statement 2: Some students are inquisitive. Statement 3: No student is inquisitive. Statement 4: Some students are not inquisitive. From the given four statements, find the two statements that CANNOT BE TRUE simultaneously, assuming that there is at least one student in the class.

solutionDiagram.alt: Four rows of small classes: all three inquisitive for statements 1 and 2, a mixed class for 2 and 4, nobody inquisitive for 3 and 4, and a question mark for statements 1 and 3 where no class works.

steps.title: What each statement says, and the rule for 'cannot be true together'
steps.body: Statement 1, 'All students are inquisitive': every student is inquisitive. Statement 2, 'Some students are inquisitive': at least one student is inquisitive, and possibly all of them. Statement 3, 'No student is inquisitive': not one student is inquisitive. Statement 4, 'Some students are not inquisitive': at least one student is not inquisitive. Two statements can be true together if you can describe one possible class, with at least one student, in which both are true. They cannot be true together only if no such class exists. So the method is to try to build a class for each offered pair.

steps.title: Build a class for the three pairs that can coexist
steps.body: Statements 1 and 2: a class of students who are all inquisitive. All are inquisitive, so at least one is. Both are true. Statements 2 and 4: a class with one inquisitive student and one who is not. Some are, and some are not. Both are true. Statements 3 and 4: a class where nobody is inquisitive. Then no student is inquisitive, and since the class is not empty, some students are not inquisitive. Both are true.

steps.title: Try the last pair
steps.body: Statements 1 and 3: Statement 1 needs every student inquisitive; Statement 3 needs every student not inquisitive. A class with at least one student would have a student who is inquisitive and not inquisitive at once. That is impossible, so no class works. The statements 'All' and 'No' are the two extremes and cannot both hold when the class is non-empty. The answer is option A.

steps.title: Why the 'at least one student' condition matters
steps.body: In an empty class, 'All students are inquisitive' and 'No student is inquisitive' are both true with nothing to check. The question rules that case out, so Statements 1 and 3 clash. The same condition is what lets Statement 3 imply Statement 4. Checking every pair by brute force over classes of up to six students confirms that the pairs which can never be true together are exactly (1,3), (1,4) and (2,3); only (1,3) is offered.

shortcut.body: Look for the pair made of 'All' and 'No'. They are the two extremes and a non-empty class cannot satisfy both. About 15 seconds. Only use this when the options contain such a pair; the other two clashing pairs, (1,4) and (2,3), are not offered here.

traps.text: Reading 'some' as 'some but not all'. In logic 'some' means at least one, and all is allowed. So a class where everyone is inquisitive makes Statements 1 and 2 both true.
Thinking 'some are inquisitive' contradicts 'some are not'. Both are true together in any mixed class, so Statements 2 and 4 are compatible.

Thinking the word 'no' in Statement 3 clashes with the word 'not' in Statement 4. In a class where nobody is inquisitive, 'some students are not inquisitive' is true, because the class has at least one student.

recognize.clues: The question gives four statements of the forms all, some, no and some-not about one group, and asks which two cannot both be true, so the task is to compare the forms of categorical statements.
recognize.contrast: This differs from a Venn validity question: there you test whether a conclusion follows from premises, here you test whether two statements are compatible, by building one class where both hold.

check.body: Count with a single student. That student is inquisitive or not. In the first case Statements 1 and 2 hold and 3 and 4 fail. In the second case Statements 3 and 4 hold and 1 and 2 fail. No one-student class makes the offered pairs of Statements 1 and 3 true together.

questions.stem: In a recently conducted national entrance test, boys constituted 65% of those who appeared for the test. Girls constituted the remaining candidates and they accounted for 60% of the qualified candidates. Which one of the following is the correct logical inference based on the information provided in the above passage?

solutionDiagram.alt: Two bars each drawn as 100 percent: the appeared bar is 65 percent boys and 35 percent girls, the qualified bar is 40 percent boys and 60 percent girls.

options: Equal number of boys and girls qualified
Equal number of boys and girls appeared for the test
The number of boys who appeared for the test is less than the number of girls who appeared
The number of boys who qualified the test is less than the number of girls who qualified

steps.title: A percentage belongs to one group
steps.body: A percentage is always a share of some group, its base. Here two groups appear: the candidates who appeared, and the candidates who qualified. '65% of those who appeared' is a share of the first group. '60% of the qualified candidates' is a share of the second. The rule: compare numbers only inside one group. The passage gives no link between the two groups, such as how many appeared or how many qualified, so a share in one group says nothing about the other.

steps.title: The group that appeared
steps.body: Boys are 65% of those who appeared, so girls are the remaining 35%. Boys outnumber girls among those who appeared. That makes option B (equal numbers appeared) false, and option C (boys fewer than girls) false.

steps.title: The group that qualified
steps.body: Girls are 60% of the qualified candidates, so boys are the other 40%. Among the qualified, girls outnumber boys. Option A (equal) is false, and option D (boys fewer than girls) is true.

steps.title: Check with numbers
steps.body: Let 1000 candidates appear, 650 boys and 350 girls, and let 300 qualify. Then 180 girls and 120 boys qualified. Girls qualified 180 of 350 and boys 120 of 650, which shows the girls' pass rate is higher, but the question needs only the shares inside each group. For any total number qualified, the girls' share 60% exceeds the boys' share 40%. The answer is option D.

shortcut.body: Read the two percentages separately: appeared 65/35 favours boys, qualified 60/40 favours girls. The only option about the qualified group that says girls are more is D. About 30 seconds. It is safe because each option names its own group; mixing the groups is the trap.

traps.text: Option A treats 60% as 'about half'. With 60% girls, the 40% boys are fewer, so the numbers are not equal.
Option B ignores the 65% figure. If equal numbers appeared, boys would be 50%, not 65%.
Option C carries the 60% of the qualified group over to those who appeared, as if girls were the majority there too. In the appeared group the boys are 65%, the larger share.

recognize.clues: The passage gives two percentages with different bases, those who appeared and the qualified candidates, and asks for the logical inference based only on the passage.
recognize.contrast: This is not a numerical-relations puzzle with one total. Here no total is given, so only statements about shares inside a single group are safe.

check.body: Pick any totals and test. With 1000 appearing and 200 qualifying, 650 boys and 350 girls appeared, and 120 girls and 80 boys qualified. With 1000 appearing and 500 qualifying, the qualified split is 300 and 200. The ordering inside each group never changes.

questions.stem: Pen : Write :: Knife : ________  Which one of the following options maintains a similar logical relation in the above?

steps.title: What an analogy asks
steps.body: 'A : B :: C : D' is read 'A is to B as C is to D'. It claims that the link between A and B is the same as the link between C and D. To solve one, state the link in a short sentence using the complete first pair, then apply that same sentence to the second pair. The answer must also be the same kind of word as B (a verb pairs with a verb, a quality with a quality).

steps.title: State the link in the first pair
steps.body: A pen is a tool, and 'write' is the action that tool is made to perform. The link is 'a tool and the action it performs'. 'Write' is a verb.

steps.title: Apply it to the knife
steps.body: A knife is a tool. The action it is made to perform is to cut. 'Cut' is a verb, like 'write'. So the blank is 'Cut'.

steps.title: Test the other options
steps.body: Vegetables is something a knife works on, an object, not the action; the matching pair for 'pen' would be 'paper'. Sharp and Blunt describe how a knife is, which are qualities, not actions. Only 'Cut' keeps the link. The answer is option C.

shortcut.body: The partner of 'Write' is a verb, so the answer must name an action. Only 'Cut' does. About 10 seconds. This works whenever one word in the given pair is clearly a verb.

traps.text: Vegetables is what a knife is used on, so it feels related. But the pair 'pen : write' links a tool to an action, not to the thing worked on; the object would be 'paper'.
Sharp is a quality of a knife, and a candidate who links the two as 'thing : property' picks it. The first pair does not give a property of the pen, so the link does not carry over.
Blunt describes a knife that cannot cut well. It is a quality and also the opposite of the useful action, so it fails both on kind and on meaning.

recognize.clues: The question is written as Pen : Write :: Knife : blank and asks for the option that keeps the same logical relation, with a verb in the first pair.
recognize.contrast: Tool and action differs from tool and object worked on. Pen goes with write, not with paper, so Knife goes with the action, not with what it cuts.

check.body: Swap in the same link from another pair. Needle goes with sew, and spoon goes with eat, both a tool and its action. The same sentence gives an action word for the knife, and only one option is an action.

questions.stem: Six students P, Q, R, S, T and U, with distinct heights, compare their heights and make the following observations. Observation I: S is taller than R. Observation II: Q is the shortest of all. Observation III: U is taller than only one student. Observation IV: T is taller than S but is not the tallest. The number of students that are taller than R is the same as the number of students shorter than ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Six bars from shortest to tallest in the order Q U R S T P, with a bracket showing three students taller than R and another showing three students shorter than S.

steps.title: Ranking by height
steps.body: The heights are all different, so the six students stand in exactly one order from shortest to tallest. Each observation limits where a student can stand. 'U is taller than only one student' means exactly one student is shorter than U. If a student stands in position k counting from the shortest as 0, then k students are shorter and 5 - k are taller. The method is to place students one by one until the whole order is fixed.

steps.title: Place Q and U
steps.body: Observation II puts Q in position 0, the shortest. Observation III says exactly one student is shorter than U, and that student must be Q (the shortest is below everyone). So U is in position 1.

steps.title: Place R, S, T and P
steps.body: Observation I gives R below S. Observation IV gives S below T and says T is not the tallest, so some student stands above T. The only student not yet placed is P, so P is the tallest. The remaining positions 2, 3, 4 hold R, S, T in that order.
steps.tex: Q < U < R < S < T < P

steps.title: Count and match
steps.body: Students taller than R: S, T and P, which is 3. We need the student who has exactly 3 students shorter. In the order Q, U, R, S, T, P, the student in position 3 is S, with Q, U and R below. T has 4 shorter, R has 2 and P has 5. The answer is S, option C.

shortcut.body: Write the order Q U R S T P in one line (about 1 minute). R has three above it, so the answer sits three places from the bottom: the fourth student, S. Unsafe if you skip the check that P is above T.

traps.text: Counting R itself among the taller students gives 4, and T has four below it. The question counts only students taller than R: S, T and P.
Naming R because it appears in the sentence. R has only two students shorter (Q and U), not three.
Placing P by guesswork. P is the tallest, so five students are shorter than P, not three.

recognize.clues: Six students with distinct heights and four comparison observations, ending in a count of students taller than one person matched with a count of students shorter than another.
recognize.contrast: This differs from a seating arrangement: there is one line of ranks and no positions around a table, so each observation is just above or below.

check.body: Test the order Q U R S T P against all four observations. S is above R, Q is lowest, U has only Q below it, and T is above S with P above T. Every observation holds, and swapping any neighbouring pair breaks one of them.

Observation III: A is shorter than D but taller than C. Observation IV: C is taller than F. Observation V: E is taller than B. The number of friends shorter than A is the same as the number of friends taller than ______.
variation.explanation: D is first, and A, C and F follow in that order because A is above C and C is above F. F has exactly two friends below it, and only E and B remain, with E above B. The order from tallest is D, A, C, F, E, B. Four friends are shorter than A (C, F, E, B), and E is the friend with exactly four taller (D, A, C, F).

questions.stem: _____ is to surgery as writer is to ________. Which one of the following options maintains a similar logical relation in the above sentence?

steps.title: What this analogy form asks
steps.body: 'X is to Y as Z is to W' says the link between X and Y is the same as the link between Z and W. Both blanks have to be filled so that the two pairs carry one link. The word that is given in each pair tells what kind of word the blank must be: 'writer' is a person who does a kind of work, so the first blank must also be a person who does a kind of work.

steps.title: Find the link
steps.body: Surgery is a piece of work done by a person, a doctor. A writer is a person whose work produces a book. So the link is 'a person and the work that person does or produces'.

steps.title: Fill both blanks
steps.body: The first blank is the person tied to surgery: Doctor. The second blank is what a writer produces: book. 'Doctor is to surgery as writer is to book.' This is option C.

steps.title: Check the others
steps.body: Plan, outline: both are things, and a plan does not perform surgery. Hospital, library: both are places, and a place does not do the work. Medicine, grammar: medicine is a field of study that contains surgery, and grammar is not what a writer produces. Only option C fits the link in both pairs.

shortcut.body: The second pair opens with 'writer', a person, so the first blank must be a person. Only 'Doctor' is a person. About 10 seconds.

traps.text: Plan and outline read like 'preparation before the work', which sounds right. But the sentence is built on 'writer', a person, so a thing-to-thing pair does not match.

Hospital is the place of surgery and a library holds books, so both pairs look like 'place and activity'. But 'writer' is a person, and a writer is not tied to a library the way surgery is tied to a hospital.

Medicine contains surgery as a branch, and grammar is something a writer uses, so each pair has a loose link. The links differ in kind: a field and its branch against a person and a tool, so the analogy fails.

recognize.clues: The sentence has two blanks, one in each pair, written as ___ is to surgery as writer is to ___, so the link must be read from both pairs together.
recognize.contrast: Person and work differs from place and activity. Surgery happens in a hospital, but the sentence names a writer, a person, so the first blank must also be a person.

check.body: Substitute the other options and read each sentence aloud. "Hospital : surgery" and "library" pair a place with a place, "Plan, outline" and "Medicine, grammar" pair things with things, and none makes a person for surgery. "Doctor : surgery :: writer : book" does, since a doctor does surgery and a writer makes a book.

Decide who carries out surgery and what a writer produces. Then check which option supplies a person for the first blank and a product for the second.

questions.stem: Given below are two statements 1 and 2, and two conclusions I and II. Statement 1: All bacteria are microorganisms. Statement 2: All pathogens are microorganisms. Conclusion I: Some pathogens are bacteria. Conclusion II: All pathogens are not bacteria. Based on the above statements and conclusions, which one of the following options is logically CORRECT?

solutionDiagram.alt: Five Venn pictures of bacteria and pathogens inside microorganisms (apart, overlapping, pathogens inside bacteria, bacteria inside pathogens, equal) with the truth of Conclusion I and Conclusion II under each.

options: Either conclusion I or II is correct.
Neither conclusion I nor II is correct.
questions.keyNote: The official key accepts both C and D. Neither conclusion is forced by itself (D), yet in every picture at least one of them is true (C), whichever way II is read, so C is the stronger logical answer and scores under the key.

steps.title: The statement forms and the Venn test
steps.body: 'All X are Y' means the set X lies completely inside the set Y. 'Some X are Y' means at least one member of X is also in Y. 'No X is Y' means the sets do not overlap. 'Some X are not Y' means at least one X lies outside Y. A conclusion is correct only if it is true in every picture that the statements allow, because the statements do not say which picture is the real one. The rule is to draw every allowed picture and test each conclusion in all of them.

steps.title: Draw every allowed picture
steps.body: Statements 1 and 2 only say that bacteria and pathogens each lie inside microorganisms. They say nothing about how the bacteria circle and the pathogen circle sit relative to each other. Five pictures are possible: (a) apart, (b) overlapping, (c) pathogens wholly inside bacteria, (d) bacteria wholly inside pathogens, (e) the two sets equal.

steps.title: Test each conclusion alone
steps.body: Conclusion I, 'some pathogens are bacteria', is true in (b), (c), (d) and (e) but false in (a). Conclusion II has two readings. As 'no pathogen is a bacterium', it is true only in (a). As 'some pathogens are not bacteria', it is true in (a), (b) and (d) and false in (c) and (e). Under either reading each conclusion fails in some picture, so neither is forced alone.

steps.title: Test the pair together
steps.body: Read II as 'no pathogen is a bacterium' and I as its opposite: exactly one of them is true in every picture. Read II as 'some pathogens are not bacteria': picture (a) makes II true, pictures (c) and (e) make I true, and (b) and (d) make both true. Either way, at least one of I and II is true in every picture, which is what 'either I or II' states. That is option C. The key also scores D, the cautious reading that neither is forced alone.

shortcut.body: Notice that I ('some pathogens are bacteria') and II ('all pathogens are not bacteria') are about the same two sets and are opposites. When two conclusions are opposites and the options include 'either I or II', choose it. About 1 minute. Be careful: if the pair were two conclusions that can both be false, the 'either or' option would be wrong.

traps.text: Taking 'Only I' because both groups sit inside microorganisms, so they seem to meet. Sharing a big set does not make two sets overlap; picture (a) keeps them apart.
Taking 'Only II' because a negative sounds safe. If every pathogen is a bacterium, as in pictures (c) and (e), II fails.

recognize.clues: Two "All ... are microorganisms" premises share one term, and the conclusions compare the two smaller groups, so the question is which conclusions hold in every Venn picture.
recognize.contrast: This is not a syllogism with a shared middle term in the predicate: the common term is the larger set, which leaves the two smaller sets free to sit in any way inside it.

check.body: Test the two extreme pictures. If the two sets are equal, every pathogen is a bacterium, so Conclusion I is true and II is false. If the two sets are apart, no pathogen is a bacterium, so I is false and II is true. Neither conclusion holds in every picture, which rules out options A and B.

questions.stem: Select the word that fits the analogy: Cook : Cook :: Fly : _____

steps.title: What an analogy asks
steps.body: 'A : B :: C : D' says A is to B as C is to D. State the link in the first pair as a sentence, then apply the same sentence to the second pair. When the two words of the first pair are spelled the same, the link cannot be a spelling change such as adding '-ing' or '-ed'; it must be a change of role.

steps.title: Find the link in 'Cook : Cook'
steps.body: The first 'cook' is the action (to cook). The second 'cook' is the person who does it (a cook). So the link is 'the action, then the person who performs it'.

steps.title: Apply it to 'Fly'
steps.body: 'Fly' is the action. The person who performs it is a flyer. Flying is the action in its -ing form, not a person. Flew is the past tense, again the action. Flighter is not an English word. The answer is option A.

shortcut.body: The partner word must name a person who does the action: only 'Flyer'. About 10 seconds.

traps.text: Flying is the -ing form of the verb. A candidate who sees 'cook : cooking' in mind picks it, but the given pair has the same spelling twice and is about a person, not a verb form.
Flew is the past tense. It would match a pair like 'cook : cooked', which changes the tense and not the role.
Flighter looks like a doer word because it ends in '-er', but it is not a word; the correct doer word for 'fly' is 'flyer'.

recognize.clues: The pair Cook : Cook repeats one spelling, so the two words differ only in their role, and the question asks for the word that fits the same link for Fly.
recognize.contrast: Verb to doer differs from verb to verb form. Cook : Cooking or Cook : Cooked would change the tense or form, but here the second word is a person.

check.body: Test the link on a second verb. Teach goes to teacher and paint goes to painter, each an action followed by the person who does it. The same test applied to Fly picks the option that names a person, and the remaining options name forms of the verb or are not words.

hints.text: Ask what role the first "Cook" plays and what role the second "Cook" plays, since the spelling is the same.
An analogy keeps one link across both pairs. When the two words look alike, the link is a change of role, not a change of spelling.
Say the link as a sentence about what the second "Cook" is to the first. Apply it to "Fly" and keep only an option that plays that same role and is a real English word.
For each option, ask what it is to "Fly" and whether that matches what the second "Cook" is to the first. Then check that the word exists.

variation.explanation: In the first pair the first word is the action and the second is the person who performs it. The doer of "dance" is a dancer. Dancing is the -ing form, danced is the past tense, and dancist is not an English word.

solutionDiagram.alt: Five boxes P Q R S T holding 3, 9, 27, 81, 243 with an arrow times 3 between neighbours, and brackets showing times 9 over each two-step gap.

steps.title: What the question gives
steps.body: The letters P, Q, R, S, T are consecutive letters, so they stand for five consecutive terms of one pattern. P, R and T are known, with Q and S missing between them. To find missing terms, look for a rule that links the known ones. Two simple rules are common: add a fixed amount each step, or multiply by a fixed ratio each step.

steps.title: Test the rule on the known terms
steps.body: P to R is two steps, and 3 becomes 27. R to T is two steps, and 27 becomes 243. If the rule were to add a fixed amount, the two gaps would match (24 each, then 216), but they do not. Multiplying fits: each two-step gap multiplies by 9.

steps.title: Find the ratio and the missing terms
steps.body: A two-step multiplication by 9 means each single step multiplies by 3, since $3 \times 3 = 9$. So Q = 3 x 3 = 9 and S = 27 x 3 = 81. The whole chain is 3, 9, 27, 81, 243, which are the powers of 3 from $3^1$ to $3^5$. A ratio of -3 would also give 9 for two steps, but then Q and S are negative, so the sum is -90, which is not offered.

steps.title: Add
steps.body: Q + S = 9 + 81 = 90. The answer is option C.

shortcut.body: Spot the powers of 3: 3, 27, 243 are $3^1, 3^3, 3^5$, so the letters in between are $3^2 = 9$ and $3^4 = 81$. Sum 90. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: 40 is near 3 + 9 + 27 = 39, the sum of the first three terms. It comes from adding the wrong terms instead of Q and S.
80 is next to S = 81 on its own. The slip is to answer with S (or S minus one) and leave Q out of the sum.
110 is near R + S = 27 + 81 = 108. The slip is to add the neighbouring pair R and S instead of Q and S.

recognize.clues: Letters stand in for terms of a sequence with the first, third and fifth given, and the question asks for the sum of the two missing terms.
recognize.contrast: An arithmetic series has equal differences. Here the differences 24 and 216 are not equal while the ratios match, so the series is geometric.

check.body: Rebuild the full chain and test the given terms. Starting at P with the found ratio, the third and fifth terms must reproduce R and T. If they do, the middle terms are right and their sum follows. A negative ratio would also fit but gives negative terms.
