hints.text: Ask what the letters P, Q, R, S and T stand for in order, and which of them the question has already given you.
A common first test for five terms in a row is whether they add a fixed amount each step or multiply by a fixed ratio. Compare the known terms to decide which.
If the rule is repeated multiplication, then going two steps multiplies by the square of the one-step ratio. Use that to find the one-step ratio from the known terms.
Divide R by P and T by R. Both two-step jumps should match. Take the square root to get the single-step ratio, then fill in Q and S from their neighbours.
Each two-step jump multiplies by 9, so a single step multiplies by 3 in magnitude. Q follows P by one step and S follows R by one step.

variation.explanation: The two-step ratio is 18 divided by 2, which is 9, and 162 divided by 18 is also 9, so each step multiplies by 3. Then Q = 2 x 3 = 6 and S = 18 x 3 = 54, and their sum is 60. The option 72 adds R and S, 24 adds Q and R, and 54 is S alone.

questions.stem: A court is to a judge as _____________ is to a teacher.

steps.title: What an analogy asks
steps.body: 'A is to B as C is to D' says the link between A and B is the same as the link between C and D. Write the link in a sentence from the pair you know, then fill in the blank so that the second pair obeys the same sentence.

steps.title: State the link
steps.body: A court is the institution where justice is done, and the judge is the person who presides over its work. The link is 'an institution and the person who conducts its work'.

steps.title: Apply it to the teacher
steps.body: A teacher conducts the work of teaching in an institution, a school. 'A school is to a teacher' keeps the link.

steps.title: Test the other options
steps.body: A student is a learner in the school, a different role from the teacher, not the institution. A punishment is something a court may order, an outcome. A syllabus is the content a teacher follows. None of these is an institution. The answer is option D.

shortcut.body: Court is a place, and the blank must be a place too. Of the four options only 'a school' is a place. About 10 seconds.

traps.text: A student sits beside the teacher in a school, so it feels paired. But the link in the first pair joins an institution with its officer, and a student is neither.
A court gives a punishment, so the word is tied to courts. The first pair links the court to the judge, and a teacher does not stand to a punishment as a judge stands to a court.
A syllabus is what a teacher follows, as a judge follows the law. That link matches 'law : judge', not 'court : judge'.

recognize.clues: The frame "A court is to a judge as ___ is to a teacher" fixes the link in the first pair and leaves the first word of the second pair blank.
recognize.contrast: A tool-and-user or cause-and-effect link would also pair a noun with a person. Here the first word is a body that the person works inside, so test the kind of word before the relation.

check.body: Read the finished pair backwards: a judge works in a court, and a teacher works in the blank. The sentence "a teacher works in a student" or "in a syllabus" is nonsense, so only a place fits the same sentence.

hints.text: Before looking at the options, say in one sentence how a court and a judge are connected.
An analogy "A is to B as C is to D" asks for the same link in both pairs, so the link matters more than the individual words.
The blank has to play the same part that "a court" plays: it must be the same kind of thing as the first word of the pair, not a thing related to the teacher in some other way.
Write the link as a sentence with a gap, such as "a judge ___ a court", then try each option in the second pair with the same sentence.

variation.stem: A bakery is to a baker as ___ is to a farmer.
variation.explanation: A bakery is the place where a baker does the work, so the blank must be the place where a farmer works. A harvest is an outcome, a tractor is a tool and a market is where produce is sold, so only a farm keeps the same link.

questions.stem: The police arrested four criminals – P, Q, R and S. The criminals knew each other. They made the following statements: P says “Q committed the crime.” Q says “S committed the crime.” R says “I did not do it.” S says “What Q said about me is false.” Assume only one of the arrested four committed the crime and only one of the statements made above is true. Who committed the crime?

solutionDiagram.alt: A truth table with one row per possible culprit P, Q, R, S and one column per statement, marked true or false, with a count of true statements; only the row for R has exactly one.

steps.title: The puzzle rule and the plan
steps.body: Each statement is either true or false. We are told two facts: exactly one person committed the crime, and exactly one of the four statements is true. The culprit is unknown, but there are only four candidates. The method: suppose each candidate in turn is the culprit, work out which statements are then true, and keep the candidate for whom exactly one statement is true.

steps.title: Turn each statement into a condition on the culprit c
steps.body: P says Q did it: true when c = Q. Q says S did it: true when c = S. R says 'I did not do it': true when c is not R. S says 'what Q said about me is false'. Q said that S did it, so S is saying that S did not do it: true when c is not S.

steps.title: Try each culprit
steps.body: c = P: R is true and S is true, so two are true. c = Q: P, R and S are true, so three. c = R: only S's statement is true, so one. c = S: Q's and R's are true, so two. Only c = R gives exactly one true statement.
steps.tex: \begin{array}{c|cccc|c} c & P & Q & R & S & \text{true} \\ \hline P & F & F & T & T & 2 \\ Q & T & F & T & T & 3 \\ R & F & F & F & T & 1 \\ S & F & T & T & F & 2 \end{array}

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: R is the culprit, option B. Check the facts: one criminal (R) and exactly one true statement (S's).

shortcut.body: Q says 'S did it' and S says 'S did not', so Q and S contradict each other and exactly one of them is true. That one true statement is the only one allowed, so P's and R's statements are false. R's statement 'I did not do it' is false, so R did it. About 30 seconds, and safe because the question promises exactly one true statement.

traps.text: Picking P because P's own statement points away from P. If P were the culprit, R's and S's statements would both be true, which breaks 'only one true'.
Picking S because Q accuses S. Then Q's statement is true, but R's 'I did not do it' is true too, giving two true statements.
Picking Q because P accuses Q. Then P's, R's and S's statements are all true, three in total.

recognize.clues: Four suspects, one culprit, and the condition that exactly one of four statements is true; S's statement refers back to Q's statement.
recognize.contrast: A knight-and-knave puzzle fixes who always lies. Here no speaker is labelled, so you cannot trust anyone and must try each suspect and count true statements.

check.body: Substitute the answer back and judge all four statements one at a time, so that you count how many are true. Then try one rejected suspect, P, and confirm that his choice leaves two statements true, which breaks the promise.

hints.text: Which two statements cannot both be true, whoever the culprit is?
Each statement is true or false depending on who committed the crime, so you can test a suspect by counting how many statements come out true.
The puzzle promises exactly one true statement. A suspect who makes zero, two or more statements true is ruled out.
Rewrite each statement as a condition on the culprit. For S, first work out what Q actually said about S, then negate it.
Q accuses S and S denies it, so one of those two statements is true and the other false. That already uses up the single true statement the puzzle allows.

variation.stem: Four suspects A, B, C and D are questioned about a theft by exactly one of them. A says "B did it." B says "I did not do it." C says "A is lying." D says "C did it." Exactly one of the four statements is true. Who committed the theft?
variation.explanation: Test each suspect and count true statements. If A did it, B's and C's statements are true. If C did it, B's, C's and D's are true. If D did it, B's and C's are true. If B did it, only A's statement is true, so B is the culprit.

questions.stem: Three of the five students allocated to a hostel put in special requests to the warden. Given the floor plan of the vacant rooms, select the allocation plan that will accommodate all their requests. Request by X: Due to pollen allergy, I want to avoid a wing next to the garden. Request by Y: I want to live as far from the washrooms as possible, since I am very sensitive to smell. Request by Z: I believe in Vaastu and so want to stay in the South-west wing. The shaded rooms are already occupied. WR is washroom.
questions.figure: Every plan is the same ring of rooms around a central compass block: 5 rows by 6 columns, written (row, column) with row 1 on top. A Garden strip runs along the whole right edge and is opened by the Entrance in row 3, column 6. The compass is a tilted cross: N at its upper left, E at its upper right, W at its lower left, S at its lower right. Washrooms WR are the rooms (1,1) and (5,1). In all four plans the occupied (shaded) rooms are (1,2) to (1,5), (2,1), (2,6), (4,1), (5,3), (5,4) and (5,6). The five free rooms are (1,6), (3,1), (4,6), (5,2) and (5,5), and the plans place X, Y, Z in three of them. (A) X (5,2), Y (5,5), Z (3,1). (B) X (1,6), Y (4,6), Z (3,1). (C) X (5,2), Y (4,6), Z (1,6). (D) X (5,2), Y (4,6), Z (5,5).

diagram.alt: Four floor plans (A) to (D): a ring of rooms around a tilted compass, washrooms at the two left corners, a garden strip on the right edge, occupied rooms shaded and the rooms of X, Y and Z marked.

solutionDiagram.alt: Plan D with the four wings named NE, SE, SW and NW and each free room marked with its distance to the nearest washroom, beside a verdict for plans A to D.

steps.title: What a wing is, and how to read a tilted compass
steps.body: A wing is one side of the ring of rooms: the top, right, bottom or left row. A compass shows where each direction points. Here the cross is drawn tilted, with N at the upper left and E at the upper right, so north is not 'up'. A side lies between two arms: the top side is between N and E, the north-east wing; the right side is between E and S, the south-east wing; the bottom side is between S and W, the south-west wing; the left side is between W and N, the north-west wing. The rule for the puzzle: a plan is correct only if all three requests hold, so test the requests one by one and drop any plan that fails.

steps.title: Z asks for the south-west wing
steps.body: The south-west wing is the bottom row. Plan (A) puts Z at (3,1) in the left wing, the north-west. Plan (B) also puts Z at (3,1), north-west. Plan (C) puts Z at (1,6) in the top row, the north-east. Plan (D) puts Z at (5,5), in the bottom row. Only (D) satisfies Z.

steps.title: Check X and Y in plan (D)
steps.body: X avoids a wing next to the garden. The garden touches the rooms in column 6 along the right edge. X is at (5,2), in the bottom row and beside the washroom, away from the garden strip. Y wants the room farthest from the washrooms. Count steps along rows and columns to the nearest washroom for each free room: (5,2) is 1, (3,1) is 2, (5,5) is 4, (1,6) is 5 and (4,6) is 6. Y is at (4,6), the largest, 6.

steps.title: Why the others fail, and the answer
steps.body: Plan (A) fails on Z, and also on Y: Y at (5,5) is only 4 steps from a washroom while (4,6) is 6. Plan (B) fails on Z, and X at (1,6) touches the garden. Plan (C) satisfies X and Y but fails on Z. Only (D) satisfies all three. The answer is option D.

shortcut.body: Start with the request that uses the compass, Z. Read the tilted cross once: south-west is the bottom side. Only plan (D) has Z in the bottom row. About 1 minute. The shortcut depends on reading the compass as tilted; if you take the top as north, you will pick the wrong plan.

traps.text: Taking the top of the page as north makes south-west the lower-left corner, and the left side looks like 'west', close to the south-west wing. Plans (A) and (B), with Z on the left side, then seem to fit. The compass here is tilted, and the left side is the north-west wing.
Plan (B) puts Y at (4,6), the farthest room, which looks right. It fails twice: X sits at (1,6) against the garden, and Z is on the left side, not in the south-west wing.
Plan (C) satisfies X and Y, so a candidate who checks only those two accepts it. Z is in the top row, the north-east wing.

recognize.clues: Z asks for a named compass wing, and the compass in the plan is drawn tilted, so the direction has to be read from the cross and not from the page.
recognize.contrast: Y's request is about distance, not direction. Count steps to the washrooms for that, and use the compass only for Z.

check.body: For the chosen plan, test all three requests independently. Z's room must lie on the side between S and W, X's room must be away from the garden strip, and Y's room must have the largest step count to a washroom among the free rooms. Then check that each rejected plan fails at least one of these.

A wing is one side of the ring of rooms, and it lies between two neighbouring arms of the compass. Name each side by the two arms it sits between.
Find the side between the arms labelled S and W, then see which plans put Z on that side. Only then test the other two requests on the plans that remain.

Each side of the ring lies between two neighbouring arms of the compass. Which side of the ring is the south-west wing?

questions.stem: There are five buildings called V, W, X, Y and Z in a row (not necessarily in that order). V is to the West of W. Z is to the East of X and the West of V. W is to the West of Y. Which is the building in the middle?

solutionDiagram.alt: Five buildings in a row from west to east in the order X, Z, V, W, Y, with V marked as the middle one and the four given relations listed below.

steps.title: What an ordering puzzle uses
steps.body: Buildings stand in a straight row that runs from West to East. 'A is to the West of B' means A comes earlier in the row than B; it says nothing about the distance between them. Each statement is one link of the form 'earlier than'. The method is to join the links that share a building into a single chain, and read off the order.

steps.title: Write each statement as a link
steps.body: V is West of W: V before W. Z is East of X: X before Z. Z is West of V: Z before V. W is West of Y: W before Y.
steps.tex: V < W,\qquad X < Z,\qquad Z < V,\qquad W < Y

steps.title: Join the links
steps.body: X < Z and Z < V share Z, giving X < Z < V. That joins V < W at V, giving X < Z < V < W. That joins W < Y at W, giving X < Z < V < W < Y. All five buildings now appear once in a single chain, so the order is fixed: X, Z, V, W, Y from west to east.

steps.title: Pick the middle
steps.body: In five places the middle is the third, which is V. The answer is option A.

shortcut.body: Chain the links in one line: X Z V W Y, then pick the third letter. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: W is the middle of the three-building chain V, W, Y that uses only the first and last statements. The other two statements put X and Z before V and push W to the fourth place.
X is the westernmost, the opposite of the middle. Picking it means 'Z is to the East of X' was read the wrong way round.
Y is the easternmost. Picking it means 'W is to the West of Y' was read as Y being west of W.

recognize.clues: Five named buildings in a row and four sentences each saying one is West or East of another, with a question about the middle position.
recognize.contrast: A circular or table seating puzzle uses left and right with neighbours. Here the row is straight and the relations are only before and after, so chaining is enough.

check.body: Write the final order from west to east and reread each of the four sentences against it, one at a time. Each must be true. Then note that every building appears exactly once, which shows the five places are all filled.

variation.stem: Five towers P, Q, R, S and T stand in a row. P is to the East of Q. R is to the West of Q. S is to the East of P. T is to the West of R. Which tower is in the middle?

questions.stem: There are three boxes. One contains apples, another contains oranges and the last one contains both apples and oranges. All three are known to be incorrectly labelled. If you are permitted to open just one box and pull out and inspect only one fruit, which box would you open to determine the contents of all three boxes?

solutionDiagram.alt: A decision tree: open the box labelled Apples and Oranges and take one fruit; an apple means that box holds only apples, an orange means it holds only oranges, and in each case the other two boxes follow.

steps.title: What a wrong label tells you
steps.body: A label is a claim about what is inside. Here every claim is false, so each label rules out one content. With three boxes and three contents, the only ways to assign contents so that no box matches its label are two. Call the boxes by their labels. First way: the 'Apples' box holds oranges, the 'Oranges' box holds the mixture, and the 'Apples and Oranges' box holds apples. Second way: the 'Apples' box holds the mixture, the 'Oranges' box holds apples, and the 'Apples and Oranges' box holds oranges. The job is to choose the box whose one fruit separates these two ways.

steps.title: Test each box
steps.body: Open the 'Apples' box: it holds oranges or the mixture. Pulling out an orange fits both ways, because the mixture also contains oranges, so you learn nothing. Open the 'Oranges' box: it holds the mixture or apples, and an apple fits both. Open the 'Apples and Oranges' box: its label is wrong, so it cannot hold the mixture. It holds only apples (first way) or only oranges (second way), and one fruit tells which.

steps.title: Finish from that one fruit
steps.body: If you pull out an apple, that box is apples only, which is the first way: the 'Oranges' box holds the mixture and the 'Apples' box holds oranges. If you pull out an orange, that box is oranges only, the second way: the 'Apples' box holds the mixture and the 'Oranges' box holds apples. One fruit fixes all three boxes. The answer is option B.

shortcut.body: Pick the box whose label names the mixture. Its label is wrong, so it is a pure box, and one fruit reveals which pure fruit it holds. The other two boxes follow because their labels are also wrong. About 30 seconds. Opening any other box leaves two possibilities.

traps.text: Opening the 'Apples' box and drawing an orange. It holds oranges or the mixture, and the mixture box contains oranges as well, so the draw cannot tell the two apart.
Opening the 'Oranges' box mirrors that slip: drawing an apple fits both the apples-only box and the mixture box.
Thinking the answer cannot be determined because one fruit seems too little. The 'every label is wrong' rule shrinks three boxes to two cases, and one draw from the right box separates them.

recognize.clues: Every label is known to be false and you may inspect only one item, so the false labels are the information to exploit.
recognize.contrast: This is not a case where you can ask a yes-or-no question. The wrong labels cut the possibilities down first, and the opened box must then separate the ones that remain.

check.body: List the two arrangements in which every box is mislabelled. Take each candidate box in turn and check whether one fruit drawn from it could occur in both arrangements. Only the chosen box gives a different fruit in the two arrangements, so it alone settles all three boxes.

Open the box whose contents, once seen, split the surviving arrangements into separate cases. A box that could hold a pure fruit or a mixture, depending on the case, tells you little.

questions.stem: Rahul, Murali, Srinivas and Arul are seated around a square table. Rahul is sitting to the left of Murali. Srinivas is sitting to the right of Arul. Which of the following pairs are seated opposite each other?

solutionDiagram.alt: A square table with Murali at the top, Rahul on the right, Srinivas at the bottom and Arul on the left, with dashed lines joining the two opposite pairs.

steps.title: Seats around a square table
steps.body: A square table has four seats, one on each side. Each person has two neighbours, one on the left and one on the right, and one person opposite. 'Left' and 'right' are taken from the point of view of the person sitting down, facing the table. 'Rahul is to the left of Murali' therefore means Rahul sits in the seat next to Murali on Murali's left hand side. The rule: a left or right link always joins neighbours, and the person opposite is the one who is not a neighbour.

steps.title: Place the four people
steps.body: Put Murali at the top, facing down. His left hand points to the right of the page, so Rahul sits at the right of the page. The two remaining seats are the bottom and the left of the page, for Srinivas and Arul. 'Srinivas is to the right of Arul' must place them as neighbours with Srinivas on Arul's right. A person on the left of the page faces right, and that person's right hand points down the page. So Arul sits on the left of the page and Srinivas at the bottom.

steps.title: Read off the opposite pairs
steps.body: Top and bottom are opposite: Murali and Srinivas. Left and right are opposite: Arul and Rahul. The mirror-image seating gives the same two pairs. The pair in the options is Srinivas and Murali, option C.

shortcut.body: Both named pairs, (Rahul, Murali) and (Srinivas, Arul), are neighbours, so options A and B are out. Between C and D, sketch the table once: Murali top, Rahul on his left, Arul on the left of the page and Srinivas on Arul's right, which puts Srinivas at the bottom, opposite Murali. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Rahul and Murali are linked by 'left of', which always joins neighbours, so they are side by side.
Srinivas and Arul are linked by 'right of', so they are neighbours as well.
Flipping one of the two links, for example putting Srinivas on Arul's left, swaps the bottom and left seats and makes Srinivas opposite Rahul.

recognize.clues: Four people around a square table, two statements each using left or right, and a question about who sits opposite.
recognize.contrast: In a straight row, left and right are fixed by the page. At a table they depend on the seated person's facing, so draw each person looking inward.

check.body: Take the finished seating and reread both statements from each person's own view, facing the table. Both must hold. Then confirm each person has exactly one person opposite and that the two opposite pairs use all four people.

questions.stem: Six people are seated around a circular table. There are at least two men and two women. There are at least three right-handed persons. Every woman has a left-handed person to her immediate right. None of the women are right-handed. The number of women at the table is

solutionDiagram.alt: Six seats round a circular table with arrows pointing to each person's immediate right: four men then two women, the two women and one man left-handed, three men right-handed.

steps.title: The rules in plain words
steps.body: At a circular table every person has exactly one person at the immediate right. Going from person to person by 'immediate right' visits all six once and returns to the start. Each person is a man or a woman, and right-handed or left-handed. The conditions are: at least 2 men, at least 2 women, at least 3 right-handed people, every woman is left-handed, and each woman's right-hand neighbour is left-handed.

steps.title: Count the left-handed people
steps.body: At least 3 of the 6 are right-handed, so at most 3 are left-handed. Every woman is left-handed. Every woman's right neighbour is also left-handed. Suppose there are $w$ women. Follow the chain of women, each handing on to her right neighbour: a woman's right neighbour is either another woman or a man. Not everyone is a woman, because there are at least 2 men, so somewhere a woman has a man on her right. That man is left-handed and is not counted among the women. So the left-handed group contains the $w$ women plus at least one man.

steps.title: Solve for the number of women
steps.body: Left-handed people number at most 3, so $w + 1 \le 3$, which gives $w \le 2$. The puzzle says there are at least 2 women, so $w = 2$.

steps.title: Check that two women can work
steps.body: Seat four men and two women in order by 'immediate right': M(left-handed), M(right), M(right), M(right), W(left), W(left). The first woman has the second woman on her right, who is left-handed. The second woman has the first man on her right, who is left-handed. There are 2 men or more, 2 women, and 3 right-handed. An enumeration of all arrangements confirms that 2 is the only number of women possible. The answer is option A.

shortcut.body: Three right-handed people leave at most 3 left-handed. The women and the man at the end of each block of women must all be left-handed, so women plus 1 is at most 3. That makes women at most 2, and the puzzle gives at least 2. About 1.5 minutes. The count 'women plus 1' needs at least one man, which the puzzle guarantees.

traps.text: Three women need at least four left-handed people (three women and the man after them), leaving only two right-handed, which breaks 'at least three right-handed'.
Four women need at least five left-handed people (four women and the man after them), leaving at most one right-handed, which breaks 'at least three right-handed'.
Thinking the data is too thin to fix the number. The cap of three left-handed people against the women-plus-one count squeezes the number to exactly 2.

recognize.clues: Six people at a circular table with conditions on right neighbours and counts of men, women and right-handed people, asking for the number of women.
recognize.contrast: A fixed-position puzzle assigns seats one by one. Here only the counting argument matters, so bound the left-handed people instead of placing everyone.

check.body: Build one explicit seating with the stated number of women and verify every condition: at least two men and women, at least three right-handed, each woman left-handed with a left-handed person on her right. Then try one more woman than the count and check that the left-handed people exceed three.

hints.text: The puzzle gives a minimum number of right-handed people. What upper limit does that put on the left-handed people?
At a round table every person has exactly one person at the immediate right, so going person to person by "immediate right" visits everyone once.
Every woman is left-handed, and so is the person on her right. Count how many left-handed people the women force, including those who are not women.
Let $w$ be the number of women. Ask who sits on the right of the last woman in a run of women, and whether that person can also be a woman.
Because there are at least two men, some woman has a man on her right, and that man is left-handed too, so the left-handed group holds more than just the women.
